newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Leaders urge work on economic part of EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Leaders urge work on economic part of EMU.

text.p: While Europeans have successfully moved towards joining their currencies, more work is necessary to hammer out the economic component of economic and monetary union (EMU), two political leaders said on Tuesday.

Recalling that EMU includes both monetary and economic pillars, Ireland's former finance minister Ruairi Quinn told a global video conference, "the issue is not monetary union but economic and monetary union."
The leaders were participating in Global 24, a global video conference on European monetary union.

Quinn applauded European nations for the work they have completed to ensure that the management of the monetary issues will be a success. This includes hammering out some technical issues as well as the design of the new currency.

But now it is essential for nations to muster the political will to "construct the economic leg which has yet to be defined," Quinn said, adding he was optimistic nations were in a position to take these steps now.

Antonio de Sousa Franco, Portugal's finance minister, added "success of monetary integration will create new needs for coordination of macro-economic policies." These should then be aimed at promoting employment," he added.

To address Europe's most pressing problem, stubbornly high unemployment levels, leaders urged more work be done to chip away at the structural problems they consider responsible for the current troubles.

While unemployment afflicts all European nations, the leaders also made clear that the root of the problem was almost always at the national level which would necessitate national programmes to solve these problems.
European institutions are not responsible for these issues, they said.
"Nobody suggests that European institutions should take on national problems on a Europe-wide level," Quinn said, adding however that the European nations should also not be silent.
